translationRepairs: On imperial summons he entered the Grand Master of Ceremonies' school, continued under the erudite Bai Qi, a classmate, and took the Analects and Mourning Dress from Xia housheng.
On imperial summons he entered the Grand Master of Ceremonies' school, continued under the erudite Bai Qi, a classmate, and took the Analects and Mourning Dress from Xiahou Sheng.
夏侯勝 is the compound surname Xiahou plus Sheng; splitting it as 'Xia housheng' is a naming error, and Xiahou Sheng is the correct English form.

By order he went to the Grand Master of Ceremonies to receive instruction, then studied again under his fellow student the erudite Bai Qi, and also questioned Xia housheng on the Analects and on Mourning Dress.

By order he went to the Grand Master of Ceremonies to receive instruction, then studied again under his fellow student the erudite Bai Qi, and also questioned Xiahou Sheng on the Analects and on Mourning Dress.
The same unit's literal also mis-segments 夏侯勝; replacing 'Xia housheng' with Xiahou Sheng restores the correct personal name.

Earlier, when Huhanye Chanyu of the Xiongnu came to court, an edict ordered the dukes and ministers to discuss the proper ritual. Chancellor Bing Ba and Imperial Counselor Yu Dingguo proposed, "In the institutions of the sage kings, virtue is extended and ritual performed first in the capital, then among the central states; first among the central states, then among the Yi and Di peoples.

Earlier, when Huhanye Chanyu of the Xiongnu came to court, an edict ordered the dukes and ministers to discuss the proper ritual. Chancellor Huang Ba and Imperial Counselor Yu Dingguo proposed, "In the institutions of the sage kings, virtue is extended and ritual performed first in the capital, then among the central states; first among the central states, then among the Yi and Di peoples.
丞相霸 has no surname Bing; earlier 黃霸代為御史大夫 and 霸為丞相 identify this chancellor as Huang Ba, so 'Bing Ba' is a false invention.
Hong Gong and Shi Xian had long run the machinery of state, knew every clause of the code, and moved in lockstep with General Wang Gao, stonewalling Wangzhi with citations of old precedent.
Hong Gong and Shi Xian had long run the machinery of state, knew every clause of the code, and moved in lockstep with General Shi Gao, stonewalling Wangzhi with citations of old precedent.
車騎將軍高 resumes 史高, earlier made 大司馬車騎將軍; 'Wang Gao' invents the wrong surname and must be Shi Gao.

Palace secretariat directors Hong Gong and Shi Xian long controlled the levers of government, were expert in written law, and also worked hand in glove with chariot-and-cavalry general Wang Gao; in debate they routinely insisted on precedent alone and would not follow Wangzhi and his allies.

Palace secretariat directors Hong Gong and Shi Xian long controlled the levers of government, were expert in written law, and also worked hand in glove with chariot-and-cavalry general Shi Gao; in debate they routinely insisted on precedent alone and would not follow Wangzhi and his allies.
Literal likewise invents surname Wang for 車騎將軍高; the prior appointment of 史高 fixes the name as Shi Gao.
Zheng Peng of Kuaiji curried favor by memorializing against General Wang Gao's clients for corruption in the provinces and against the Xu and Shi clans.
Zheng Peng of Kuaiji curried favor by memorializing against General Shi Gao's clients for corruption in the provinces and against the Xu and Shi clans.
車騎將軍高 again refers to Shi Gao; 'Wang Gao' is the same invented surname and should be corrected.

Zheng Peng of Kuaiji covertly wished to attach himself to Wangzhi; he submitted a memorial charging that chariot-and-cavalry general Wang Gao had sent agents to pursue illicit profit in the commanderies and kingdoms, and also detailing faults of the Xu and Shi younger kin.

Zheng Peng of Kuaiji covertly wished to attach himself to Wangzhi; he submitted a memorial charging that chariot-and-cavalry general Shi Gao had sent agents to pursue illicit profit in the commanderies and kingdoms, and also detailing faults of the Xu and Shi younger kin.
The literal of the same memorial likewise misnames 車騎將軍高 as Wang Gao; Shi Gao is required by the chapter's earlier identification.

He earned promotion to Chenliu by crushing the Jiangxia bandit Cheng Zhong; in Yuanshi, when the Bright Hall rose and lords gathered in court, he was called to be grand herald but took ill, missed the rites, went back to his old post, and retired sick.

For his merit in suppressing Cheng Zhong and the other river bandits, he was raised in rank and appointed governor of Chenliu. In the Yuanshi era, when the Bright Hall and Circular Moat were built and the feudal lords assembled at a grand court, he was summoned as Grand Herald. Illness kept him from presiding over the reception, so he returned to his former post and was later dismissed on grounds of illness.

The source has river bandits rather than a Jiangxia bandit, includes Cheng Zhong's companions and the Circular Moat, and says illness prevented Xiao You from performing the reception duties. The worker found the omissions, but its proposed English was too literal for the idiomatic field.
Otherwise this towering Confucian, broken yet unbowed, might have been the sort of pillar who steadies the altars of state in recent times.

Had things turned out otherwise, the imposing Wangzhi—broken but never bent, a master of the Confucian tradition with the ability to aid a ruler—would have ranked among the great ministers of the state in recent antiquity.
不然 introduces a counterfactual and the sentence explicitly names Wangzhi. The worker correctly restored those points, but its proposed tense and repeated 'altars' were unnatural in English.
Wangzhi, going out from junior privy treasurer to the left side, feared it was a demotion for displeasing the ruler, and immediately pleaded illness.
Wangzhi regarded leaving the acting Privy Treasurer's office for the Left Fengyi as a demotion; fearing that he had somehow displeased the emperor, he immediately pleaded illness.
Clarifies that Wangzhi regarded the transfer from acting Privy Treasurer to Left Fengyi as a demotion; the emperor had not assigned Xuancheng or removed him for misconduct.
He read the move from privy treasurer to "left" as a demotion for having offended the throne and at once filed a sick note.
Wangzhi regarded his transfer from acting Privy Treasurer to Left Fengyi as a demotion and, fearing he had displeased the emperor, immediately reported himself ill.
Clarifies that Wangzhi regarded the transfer from acting Privy Treasurer to Left Fengyi as a demotion; the emperor had not assigned Xuancheng or removed him for misconduct.

as for harboring fugitives, "see and know" indulgence, and acts that ought not to be done—some debaters have even said their laws might be abolished; now by this order to ransom, the convenience is very clear—where is the confusion of transformation?

As for harboring offenders, knowingly allowing crimes, and other offenses of that kind, some advisers have argued that the statutes might be abolished. Allowing redemption in these cases would plainly be beneficial; how would it disrupt moral education?
Corrects the legal categories and the argument that redeeming these sentences would not damage moral education.
while harboring, "see-know" liability, and similar statutes some would repeal would gain a clear outlet. How would civilization suffer?

As for harboring offenders, knowingly allowing crimes, and similar offenses, some advisers have even argued that the statutes should be abolished. Letting such offenders redeem their sentences would plainly be beneficial. How would that damage moral education?
Corrects the legal categories and the argument that redeeming these sentences would not damage moral education.

I have heard that in the fourth year of Tianhan it was customary to have men sentenced to death pay five hundred thousand cash to reduce capital crime one grade; powerful magnates among officials and commoners borrowed and seized on false pretenses (the text is damaged here), to the point of becoming bandits in order to ransom crimes.

I have heard that in the fourth year of Tianhan, people sentenced to death were allowed to pay five hundred thousand cash to reduce the sentence by one degree. Powerful officials and commoners solicited, seized, borrowed, and took loans, even becoming bandits in order to redeem their crimes.
Restores the damaged reading 假貸 and distinguishes soliciting, seizure, borrowing, and loans used to raise redemption money.

We are told that in Tianhan 4 men under death sentence could pay five hundred thousand cash to commute one degree; magnates borrowed, seized, and forged credentials until some turned bandit to raise the fee.

We are told that in Tianhan 4, people under sentence of death could pay five hundred thousand cash to commute the penalty by one degree. Powerful officials and commoners solicited, seized, borrowed, and took loans to raise the money; some even turned to banditry to redeem their crimes.
Restores the damaged reading 假貸 and distinguishes soliciting, seizure, borrowing, and loans used to raise redemption money.

Earlier, the Wusun great chanyu Wengguimi, through the marquis of Changluo, Chang Hui, had submitted a memorial, wishing to make his Han-born grandson Yuanguimi heir, to be able again to marry the young princess, bind marriage and attach inward, and turn away from the Xiongnu.

Earlier, Wengguimi, Kunmi of Wusun, had submitted a memorial through Chang Hui, Marquis of Changluo, asking that Yuanguimi, a maternal grandson of Han, succeed him and in turn marry the Lesser Princess, renewing the marriage alliance, attaching Wusun to Han, and breaking with the Xiongnu.
Corrects the Wusun succession, parentage, Lesser Princess, and proposed marriage alliance.
Earlier the Wusun ruler Wengguimi had petitioned through Marquis Chang Hui to install his part-Han grandson Yuanguimi and remarry the imperial princess, cleaving to Han and away from the Xiongnu.

Earlier Wengguimi, Kunmi of Wusun, had petitioned through Chang Hui, Marquis of Changluo, asking that his son Yuanguimi, a grandson of the Han imperial house through his mother, succeed him and marry the Lesser Princess. This would renew the marriage alliance, attach Wusun to Han, and sever its ties with the Xiongnu.
Corrects the Wusun succession, parentage, Lesser Princess, and proposed marriage alliance.
Formerly the young princess was in Wusun more than forty years; intimacy and affection were not close; the borderlands were not thereby secure—this is verification from what has already happened.
The previous princess lived in Wusun for more than forty years, yet affection between the two sides was not close and the frontier was not thereby secured. The past already proves the point.
Distinguishes Princess Jieyou, the previous princess, from the current Lesser Princess.
The last princess dwelt there forty years without real intimacy or a quiet border—that is the precedent.
The previous princess lived in Wusun for more than forty years, yet the alliance never became close and the frontier never became secure. The past already proves the point.
Distinguishes Princess Jieyou, the previous princess, from the current Lesser Princess.
Later Wusun though split into two states enthroned with Yuanguimi as great chanyu, and Han thereafter did not again bind marriage with them.
Later, although Wusun split into two realms and Yuanguimi was established as the senior Kunmi, Han never again formed a marriage alliance with Wusun.
Corrects 大昆彌 to senior Kunmi rather than chanyu.
Wusun later split into two courts with Yuanguimi as great chanyu, and Han never again married into the line.
Wusun later split into two realms, with Yuanguimi as the senior Kunmi, and Han never again renewed the marriage alliance.
Corrects 大昆彌 to senior Kunmi rather than chanyu.

An edict dispatched the grand marshal and chariot-and-cavalry general Han Zeng of the inner court, the various officials and marquis of Fuping Zhang Yanshou, superintendent of the household Yang Yun, and grand coachman Dai Changle to ask Wangzhi for plans; Wangzhi replied, saying, "The Spring and Autumn Annals condemns Shi Hui (the graph in the text is damaged) leading troops to invade Qi; hearing that the marquis of Qi had died, he led the army back; the gentleman praises him for not attacking mourning, holding that kindness is sufficient to subdue filial sons and righteousness sufficient to move the feudal lords.

An edict dispatched Grand Marshal and Chariot-and-Cavalry General Han Zeng of the inner court, Zhang Yanshou, Marquis of Fuping, Minister of the Household Yang Yun, and Grand Coachman Dai Changle to ask Wangzhi for a plan. Wangzhi replied, "The Spring and Autumn Annals censures Shi Gai for leading an army to invade Qi. When he heard that the Marquis of Qi had died, he withdrew his army. The noble man praises his refusal to attack a state in mourning, holding that such kindness could win over filial sons and such righteousness could move the feudal lords.
Restores 士匄 as Shi Gai and clarifies the Spring and Autumn precedent.

The court sent Grand Marshal Han Zeng, Marquis Zhang Yanshou of Fuping, Yang Yun, and Dai Changle to ask his counsel. Wangzhi answered: "The Annals fault Shi Hui for invading Qi with an army; when he learned the marquis had died, he withdrew. The noble man exalts refusing to strike a mourner—grace that wins filial sons and duty that sways the lords.

The court sent Grand Marshal Han Zeng, Zhang Yanshou, Marquis of Fuping, Yang Yun, and Dai Changle to ask his counsel. Wangzhi answered: "The Annals censures Shi Gai for leading an army against Qi. When he learned that the Marquis of Qi had died, he withdrew. Yet the noble man praises his refusal to attack a state in mourning: kindness enough to win over filial sons, righteousness enough to move the lords.
Restores 士匄 as Shi Gai and clarifies the Spring and Autumn precedent.
At that time the grand minister of agriculture and palace assistant Geng Shouchang memorialized to establish ever-normal granaries; the emperor approved it; Wangzhi opposed Shouchang.

At that time Geng Shouchang, Deputy Director in the Office of the Grand Minister of Agriculture, memorialized in favor of establishing ever-normal granaries. The emperor approved, but Wangzhi opposed Shouchang.
Parses 大司農中丞 as Deputy Director under the Grand Minister of Agriculture.
When Grand Minister of Agriculture Geng Shouchang proposed ever-normal granaries, the emperor liked the idea; Wangzhi attacked it.
When Geng Shouchang, Deputy Director under the Grand Minister of Agriculture, proposed ever-normal granaries, the emperor approved the plan, but Wangzhi opposed it.
Parses 大司農中丞 as Deputy Director under the Grand Minister of Agriculture.

The emperor, because Wangzhi's meaning slighted the chancellor, thereupon sent down the attendant-in-chamber and commandant of the guards of Jianzhang Jin An'shang, superintendent of the household Yang Yun, and palace secretary Wang Zhong together to interrogate Wangzhi.

The emperor took Wangzhi's memorial as a slight to the chancellor and ordered Palace Attendant and Jianzhang Guard Commandant Jin An'shang, Minister of the Household Yang Yun, and Wang Zhong, Palace Aide to the Imperial Counselor, to question Wangzhi together.
Corrects Wang Zhong's office to Palace Aide to the Imperial Counselor.
Reading this as a snub to the chancellor, the emperor set Jin An'shang, Yang Yun, and Palace Secretary Wang Zhong to question him jointly.
Taking the memorial as a slight to the chancellor, the emperor ordered Jin An'shang, Yang Yun, and Wang Zhong, Palace Aide to the Imperial Counselor, to question Wangzhi jointly.
Corrects Wang Zhong's office to Palace Aide to the Imperial Counselor.
A junior clerk wore the statutory cap, went ahead to lead his wife, and also ran purchases for him; private additions to his wealth totaled 103,000 cash.
He had a junior clerk wear the law cap and go ahead to clear the way for his wife, and also used him to conduct purchases and sales; the private benefit amounted to 103,000 cash.
Clarifies the private misuse of a junior clerk and the resulting financial benefit.
A junior clerk wore the law cap, led his wife about, and brokered deals for him, padding private accounts by 103,000 cash.
He had a junior clerk put on the law cap and clear the way for his wife, and used the clerk to handle private buying and selling that benefited him by 103,000 cash.
Clarifies the private misuse of a junior clerk and the resulting financial benefit.

Consider Wangzhi: a great minister, versed in the classics, seated above the nine ministers, on whom the court relies—to reach the point of refusing to keep the law or discipline himself, of crouching in arrogance and insubordination, and of taking more than 250 cash in illicit gains from those he oversaw: we request his arrest and trial."

Wangzhi is a great minister, versed in the classics, ranked above the nine ministers, and looked up to by the court. Yet he failed to observe the law or discipline himself, behaved with arrogant insubordination, and received illicit goods worth 250 cash or more from people under his supervision. We request his arrest and trial."
Corrects the statutory threshold: illicit goods worth 250 cash or more from persons under Wangzhi's supervision.

He was a pillar of state, steeped in the classics and ranked above the nine ministers, yet he flouted the law, behaved with arrogant insubordination, and pocketed over 250 cash from subordinates—arrest and trial are in order."

Wangzhi was a pillar of state, steeped in the classics and ranked above the nine ministers, yet he flouted the law, behaved with arrogant insubordination, and accepted illicit goods worth at least 250 cash from people under his supervision. We request his arrest and trial."
Corrects the statutory threshold: illicit goods worth 250 cash or more from persons under Wangzhi's supervision.

When Emperor Xuan fell gravely ill, he chose great ministers to whom he could entrust affairs, summoned his maternal kinsman Palace Attendant Yueling Marquis Shi Gao, heir-apparent tutor Wangzhi, and junior tutor Zhou Kan to the inner palace, appointed Gao grand marshal and chariot-and-cavalry general, Wangzhi forward general and superintendent of the household, and Kan grand master of the household; all received the dying edict to assist government and oversaw Masters of Writing affairs.

When Emperor Xuan fell gravely ill, he selected great ministers to whom he could entrust affairs and summoned to the inner palace his maternal kinsman Shi Gao, Palace Attendant and Marquis of Leling; Wangzhi, Grand Tutor to the Heir Apparent; and Zhou Kan, Junior Tutor. He appointed Shi Gao Grand Marshal and Chariot-and-Cavalry General, Wangzhi Forward General and Minister of the Household, and Zhou Kan Grandee of Splendid Light. All received the deathbed edict to assist the government and take charge of Secretariat affairs.
Corrects Shi Gao's fief to Leling and normalizes the regents' offices.

When Emperor Xuan fell gravely ill, he chose ministers to whom he could entrust the realm, summoned his maternal kinsman Palace Attendant Yueling Marquis Shi Gao, crown-prince tutor Wangzhi, and junior tutor Zhou Kan to the inner palace, made Gao grand marshal and general of chariots and cavalry, Wangzhi forward general and superintendent of the household, and Kan grand master of the household; all received the deathbed edict to assist government and headed Secretariat affairs.

When Emperor Xuan fell gravely ill, he chose ministers to whom he could entrust the realm. He summoned his maternal kinsman Shi Gao, Palace Attendant and Marquis of Leling, together with Crown Prince Tutor Wangzhi and Junior Tutor Zhou Kan. Shi Gao was made Grand Marshal and Chariot-and-Cavalry General, Wangzhi Forward General and Minister of the Household, and Zhou Kan Grandee of Splendid Light. All three received the deathbed edict to assist the government and direct the Secretariat.
Corrects Shi Gao's fief to Leling and normalizes the regents' offices.
Under Emperor Xuan the court favored law over Confucian rhetoric, and eunuch directors of the secretariat held real leverage.
Under Emperor Xuan the court favored legal administration over Confucian learning, and eunuchs in the palace secretariat wielded real power.
Restores the contrast between Confucian learning and legal administration.

Wangzhi argued that the secretariat was the administrative heart and should be manned by scholars; since Emperor Wu's harem diversions, castrates had filled those desks—neither ancient practice nor wise policy—and he pressed to put gentlemen in their place, making bitter enemies of Gao, Gong, and Xian.

Wangzhi argued that the secretariat was the heart of government and should be staffed by worthy, capable men. Eunuchs had been employed there since Emperor Wu began visiting and holding banquets in the rear palace, but this was neither an original Han institution nor consistent with the ancient principle of keeping punished men at a distance. He proposed replacing them with regular officials, bringing him into sharp conflict with Shi Gao, Hong Gong, and Shi Xian.
Clarifies why eunuchs entered the secretariat and identifies Wangzhi's institutional proposal.
The young emperor shrank from sweeping reform; while debate stalled, Liu Gengsheng was parked in the Directorate of Imperial Clan Affairs.
Newly enthroned, the emperor was reluctant to make sweeping changes. While the debate remained unresolved, Liu Gengsheng was transferred out to serve as Director of the Imperial Clan.
Corrects Liu Gengsheng's transfer to Director of the Imperial Clan.
Zhou Kan read the paper, forwarded it, and had Peng posted as an expectant scholar at the Golden Horse Gate.
The memorial was shown to Zhou Kan, who reported it to the emperor and had Peng appointed to await imperial summons at the Golden Horse Gate.
Corrects the pronoun: Zheng Peng's memorial was shown to Zhou Kan.
Wangzhi, having accepted Peng, received him according to inclination.
Wangzhi accepted Peng and received him with favor.
Removes unsupported colloquial characterization while preserving Wangzhi's acceptance of Peng.
Wangzhi took the bait and treated Peng with cordial favor.
Wangzhi welcomed Peng and treated him with favor.
Removes unsupported colloquial characterization while preserving Wangzhi's acceptance of Peng.
Xian and Gong feared Wangzhi would plead his own case, so they sent the matter down to other officials and at once enlisted Peng and attendant Hua Long.

Shi Xian and Hong Gong feared that Wangzhi would defend himself and that the matter would then be referred to other officials, so they immediately brought pressure to bear on Peng and Hua Long, who was awaiting imperial summons.
Corrects the causal sequence: the eunuchs feared an independent inquiry and therefore pressured Peng and Hua Long.
Shi Xian and Hong Gong feared Wangzhi would defend himself in court, so they referred the case to other officials and at once enlisted Peng and attendant Hua Long.

Shi Xian and Hong Gong feared that Wangzhi would defend himself and the case would be handed to other officials. They therefore pressured Peng and Hua Long, another man awaiting imperial summons, into acting against him.
Corrects the causal sequence: the eunuchs feared an independent inquiry and therefore pressured Peng and Hua Long.

Let him be granted rank of marquis within the passes, sustenance of six hundred households, attendant within the yellow gates, audience at the new and full moons, seating next below the generals." The Son of Heaven was on the point of relying on him to make him chancellor, when Wangzhi's son Ren, gentleman rider at large, submitted a memorial disputing Wangzhi's earlier case; the matter went to the offices, which reported again: "What Wangzhi was earlier charged with was clear; there was no false accuser; yet he taught his son to memorialize, citing an Ode that speaks of innocence—he lost the bearing of a great minister; it is irreverent; we request arrest."

Let Wangzhi be granted the rank of Marquis within the Passes, an estate of six hundred households, the status of Palace Attendant, audience at the new and full moons, and a seat immediately below the generals." The emperor was then relying on Wangzhi and intended to make him chancellor. Just then Wangzhi's son Ji, a Gentleman of the Cavalry, submitted a memorial disputing his father's former case. The matter was referred to the responsible offices, which again reported: "The charges on which Wangzhi was previously convicted are clear, and no one falsely accused him. Yet he instructed his son to memorialize and cite an Ode proclaiming innocence. This violates the bearing of a great minister and is disrespectful. We request his arrest."
Restores Xiao Ji's name and clarifies the restoration, memorial, and renewed arrest request.

He awarded Wangzhi marquis-within-the-passes rank, six hundred households, palace attendant status, audiences on the new and full moons, and a seat just below the generals." The emperor had meant to raise him to chancellor, but his son Ren, a gentleman rider, petitioned to reopen an old case; the ministries replied that the earlier verdict was sound, that no one had slandered him, yet teaching a son to quote the Odes on innocence was unworthy of a great minister—disrespect—and asked for his arrest.

Let Wangzhi be granted the rank of Marquis within the Passes, an estate of six hundred households, the status of Palace Attendant, audiences at the new and full moons, and a seat immediately below the generals." The emperor was then relying on Wangzhi and intended to make him chancellor. Just then Wangzhi's son Ji, a Gentleman of the Cavalry, petitioned to reopen his father's former case. The responsible offices replied that the earlier charges were clear and no one had slandered him; by instructing his son to submit a memorial and quote an Ode proclaiming innocence, Wangzhi had violated the bearing of a great minister and shown disrespect. They requested his arrest.
Restores Xiao Ji's name and clarifies the restoration, memorial, and renewed arrest request.
Wangzhi reached for poison; his wife restrained him, sure the emperor could not mean it.
Wangzhi wanted to kill himself, but his wife stopped him, convinced that this could not be the emperor's intention.
Preserves the wife's intervention without adding an unsupported action involving poison.
He addressed him by style, saying to Yun, "You—hurry and bring the mixed poison; do not long delay my death!"
Addressing Zhu Yun by his courtesy name, he said, "You, hurry and bring the prepared poison. Do not delay my death!"
Clarifies that You is Zhu Yun's courtesy name and keeps the command's addressee explicit.
Calling him by his style, "You," he said, "fetch the draught at once—do not make me wait in shame!"
Addressing Zhu Yun by his courtesy name, Wangzhi said, "You, hurry and bring the poison. Do not keep me waiting to die!"
Clarifies that You is Zhu Yun's courtesy name and keeps the command's addressee explicit.
When the Son of Heaven heard it he was startled; clapping his hands he said, "Earlier We indeed doubted he would not submit to prison; in the end he has killed Our worthy tutor!"
When the emperor heard, he was startled and struck his hands together: "I suspected from the first that he would not submit to imprisonment. They have indeed killed my worthy tutor!"

The emperor struck his palm and groaned, "We feared he would never endure a cell—he has murdered Our finest teacher!"
